newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court sends Papon to trial for war crimes.
newsitem.headline: French court sends Papon to trial for war crimes.

text.p: A French appeals court on Wednesday ordered former cabinet minister Maurice Papon, 86, to stand trial for crimes against humanity for sending Jews from wartime France to their deaths in Nazi extermination camps.

He was only the second Frenchman to be sent to trial for such crimes. A lower-ranking collaborator, former militia officer Paul Touvier, was jailed for life in 1994, and died in prison this year aged 81.

Papon, who rose to be Paris police chief in the 1960s and a Gaullist budget minister in the 1970s before his World War Two role was exposed, is accused of having ordered the deportation of 1,690 Jews, including 223 children, in 1942-44 when he was secretary-general of the Bordeaux regional administration.
Most were later gassed at the Auschwitz death camp.
The Bordeaux court sent Papon to a jury trial in an assize court on charges of being an accomplice to the murder and kidnapping of 10 convoys of deportees.
His lawyer immediately appealed to the Supreme Court against the ruling, which follows 15 years of procedural battles since relatives of the victims started legal action.

At hearings in the appeals court last March, the public prosecutor said Papon was responsible for sending Jews on four trains which left Drancy, near Paris, for the death camps in 1942 and 1944. Lawyers for relatives of the victims held him responsible for six more trains.
The prosecutor said Papon must have known about Hitler's "final solution" -- the extermination of the Jews of Europe by the Nazis -- although he had no evidence to back this.
Papon is probably the last French official to face such charges more than half a century after the end of the war.
His lawyer, Jean-Marc Varaut, argued that the former minister never followed Nazi ideology and had only obeyed orders imposed by the occupying power.
He said Papon could thus not be accused of crimes against humanity, the only charge that is not covered by the statute of limitations, and the court should drop the case.
After the ruling, Varaut said he was bitterly disappointed, especially since the court had gone beyond the prosecution's request and added charges sought by the civil plaintiffs.
